name: Colin Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the rebuild crew for the dry hill country round Red Gully. When a wildfire goes through, it takes the wooden poles with it, and we go in after the fire crews and put the whole line back up, sometimes twenty kilometres of it. The ground's black, the air smells of smoke for weeks, and the farmers are desperate to get their pumps going again. Between fires we do the normal stuff: maintenance, replacing old poles with steel ones that won't burn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does a typical day start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six o'clock at the yard, coffee, and I go through the job on my phone. I take photos of the burnt line the day before and get an AI tool to count the poles, mark which ones are gone and draft the materials list. It's not perfect, but it's a two-hour job done in twenty minutes. The foreman thought I was cheating till he checked it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Joanne, my wife, does the books for a few farms. Our daughter got married last year, and two years ago I lost a chunk of our savings on a cryptocurrency thing that went to nothing, so there's about three weeks in the bank. That was my mistake and I own it. The rebuild crew pays less than the city depots, and there's no other line work out here. We're at the chapel most Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame, because I've had a lot of use out of it. I'd tell the lads it still saves me two hours a job, so it's worth learning. I'd probably post a video of how I do the materials list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes. I keep my job, keep using the tools, keep working to sixty-six. The money problem is my own doing, and AI wasn't going to fix that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep pitching the foreman on using the photo tool for the whole crew. And I'd start a little side line doing private poles for farmers, the ones they own themselves on their land, on weekends, to rebuild what I lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, honestly, I like a bit of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the cryptocurrency loss. Has it changed how you take risks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With money, a bit. I don't put in what I can't lose now. But I still think the man who tries things does better than the man who sits still, as long as he learns from his mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the farmers trust you for private work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of them know me from the fires. Old Ted Burrows has been on at me for a year to replace his three poles before the next fire season. That's a weekend's work and a decent bit of money.

S0.say: I'd say that's a shame because the tools save me two hours a job, so they're still worth learning. I'd probably post a video of how I do the materials list.
S0.think: For me not much changes: I keep the job, use the tools and work to sixty-six. My money problem is my own doing, and AI wasn't going to fix it.
S0.do: Keeps working and pitches the photo tool to the whole crew. Starts a weekend side line replacing farmers' private poles to rebuild his savings.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat because he likes change.
S0.quote: I don't put in what I can't lose now.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is a daily AI user who owns his past money mistake rather than blaming anyone. His free-market outlook shows in his instinct to start a side business. He likes change and is slightly bored by a world without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for anyone willing to learn. The work's changing, so change with it. Nobody owes us a living, and the people who move first will do best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of it. If drones and software can survey a burnt line, someone has to fly them, check the data and sign it off, and I'm already halfway there. I'm fifty-eight, but I learn fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a decent drone in the first few months, maybe two thousand, on a payment plan, and get the licence. I'd offer fire damage surveys to the company as a contractor and to farmers privately. I'd use the AI tools to write the reports and do the quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous about the payment plan, after last time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody owes us a living. What about older colleagues who can't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a fair push. I'd help them, I'd teach anyone who asked. But I don't think the government should pay people to stand still. Better the company runs proper apprenticeships for older workers too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A payment plan, after losing your savings. Is that a risk you'd really take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because this time it's a tool I'd use, not a gamble. A drone earns its keep or it doesn't, and I can see the work coming. Joanne would want to see the numbers first, and she'd be right.

S1.say: I'd say this is good news for anyone willing to learn, because nobody owes us a living. The people who move first will do best.
S1.think: I think I'd do well out of it, since someone has to fly the survey drones, check the data and sign it off, and I'm halfway there. I learn fast even at fifty-eight.
S1.do: Buys a drone for about two thousand on a payment plan in the first few months and gets the licence. Offers fire damage surveys to the company as a contractor and to farmers privately, using AI tools for reports and quotes.
S1.feel: Excited, with some nerves about borrowing again.
S1.quote: This time it's a tool I'd use, not a gamble. A drone earns its keep or it doesn't
S1.fieldNote: Colin sees steady change as a business opening and acts fast, even borrowing again after a past loss. When pushed on older colleagues he offers help and apprenticeships rather than government support. He knows his wife would check the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, and I'd say it fast. I wouldn't want the government stopping it, but I'd want companies to keep their older people on long enough to retrain. I'd say that online and at the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years worries me more than I'd let on. If robots can do the rebuilds and the drones fly themselves, my survey business has a year, maybe two, before it's not needed either. I'd be sixty with three weeks in the bank and a payment plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still start the survey business, straight away, to get what I can while it lasts. I'd cut back hard at home, no holidays, no new truck. And I'd look for work helping set up and repair the robots, because they'll break out in the hills and someone will have to fetch them out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be moving fast, but I'd be anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's no runway. With five or ten years I could build something that lasts till I retire. With two, I'm grabbing what I can and hoping it carries me to sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look for robot repair work. Is that realistic at sixty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, more than people think. Robots in the hills will get stuck in creek beds and covered in ash. They'll need someone who knows the country and isn't scared of a manual, and that's me.

S2.say: I'd say adapt or get left behind, and fast. I wouldn't want the government stopping it, but I'd want companies to keep older people on long enough to retrain.
S2.think: Two years worries me more than I'd let on, because my survey business would only last a year or two before the robots and self-flying drones made it unnecessary. I'd be sixty with three weeks in the bank and a payment plan.
S2.do: Starts the survey business straight away to earn while it lasts and cuts back hard at home, dropping holidays and a new truck. Looks for work setting up and fixing the robots out in the hills.
S2.quote: Robots in the hills will get stuck in creek beds and covered in ash.
S2.fieldNote: Even Colin's appetite for change runs short of time in the two-year picture. His plan shifts from building something lasting to grabbing what he can. His idea of fixing robots out in the hills shows he still looks for a role rather than help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone who wants to get ready. Learn the new kit, look for where the work's going. I'd say it to the younger lads especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three, and I think that's a good run. I could build the survey business, then move into robot repair work, and still have money coming in till near the pension. I'd feel all right about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, the drone and the licence, and start the surveys on weekends. Year two, I'd look for any course on maintaining the new robots, and I'd use the AI to study for it. I'd pay off the drone first, then start putting money away properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, and keen to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me build in steps instead of jumping. Two years is a leap in the dark. Five years is a ladder, one rung at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Joanne say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say slow down and show her the spreadsheet. Then she'd do the books for the survey business, because she's better at that than me. We'd be a team, like we are with everything.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone who wants to get ready, so learn the new kit and follow the work. I'd say it to the younger lads especially.
S3.think: Five years takes me to sixty-three, which is a good run: build the survey business, move into robot repair and keep money coming in till near the pension. I'd feel all right about it.
S3.do: Buys the drone, gets the licence and starts weekend surveys in year one, then takes a robot maintenance course in year two, studying with AI. Pays off the drone first, then starts saving properly.
S3.feel: Mostly calm and keen to get started.
S3.quote: Two years is a leap in the dark. Five years is a ladder, one rung at a time.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Colin the stepwise path he wants, and his mood settles. His wife acts as a check on his risk-taking and would run the business books. He frames everything as personal effort and teamwork at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. Learn, save, plan. I'd say it at the yard and at chapel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight. I'd probably still be doing a bit of survey or repair work because I enjoy it, not because I have to. It's my daughter's generation who'll need to think hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan as the five-year one, just slower and safer: drone, licence, surveys, robot course. I'd save more steadily and pay off the payment plan first. And I'd help my son-in-law, who's an apprentice electrician, get onto the new kit early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested to see how it plays out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would shake that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another fire season like 2019, when we worked eighteen days straight. My body's not what it was. If I got hurt, all the plans would wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rather have the ten years or the two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten. I like change, but I'm not twenty-five. At my age, time is the thing you can't buy.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it to learn, save and plan. I'd say it at the yard and at chapel.
S4.think: I'd be sixty-eight, probably doing a bit of survey or repair work for enjoyment rather than need. My daughter's generation are the ones who will need to think hard.
S4.do: Follows the same drone, licence, survey and robot course plan, but slower and safer. Pays off the payment plan first, saves steadily and helps his electrician son-in-law get onto the new kit early.
S4.quote: At my age, time is the thing you can't buy.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Colin is relaxed and focuses on helping his son-in-law. The one threat he names is his body during a bad fire season. Even someone who loves change prefers the long runway at his age.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is companies keeping older workers on long enough to retrain, and paying for the courses, rather than the government paying people to sit at home. Give me a course and a bit of time and I'll sort myself out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's to blame. I don't think anyone is. It's like a fire: no point shouting at it, you get your boots on.

headlineQuote: It's like a fire: no point shouting at it, you get your boots on.
portrait: Colin Abbott is a fifty-eight-year-old lineworker on a wildfire rebuild crew in dry hill country, putting burnt lines back up for farmers. He uses AI every day to count damaged poles from photos and draft materials lists, but a cryptocurrency loss he openly owns left him with about three weeks of savings. He believes in self-reliance, work and apprenticeships rather than handouts, and goes to chapel most Sundays. He is calm in the mild pictures and quick to start a drone survey business, anxious only when AGI arrives in two years, and calm again with five or ten years, which he sees as a ladder he can climb one rung at a time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his survey business would only last a year or two and he'd be sixty with little savings and a payment plan.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping older workers on long enough to retrain and paying for the courses, rather than government paying people to stay home.
